question: Which suburbs had the fastest rent growth last year?
answer: Rent growth for NSW suburbs over the past year.
sql:
WITH ym AS (
  SELECT EXTRACT(YEAR FROM month)*12 + EXTRACT(MONTH FROM month) AS mk, month FROM marts.property_rent
),
maxym AS (
  SELECT MAX(EXTRACT(YEAR FROM month)*12 + EXTRACT(MONTH FROM month)) AS mx FROM marts.property_rent
),
rent_by_postcode AS (
  SELECT postcode, month, SUM(total_weekly_rent) AS total_rent, SUM(n_rented) AS n_rented
  FROM marts.property_rent
  GROUP BY postcode, month
),
suburb_rent AS (
  SELECT g.suburb, r.month,
         SUM(r.total_rent) AS total_rent,
         SUM(r.n_rented) AS n_rented
  FROM rent_by_postcode r
  JOIN staging.int_postcode_geo g ON r.postcode = g.postcode
  GROUP BY g.suburb, r.month
),
recent AS (
  SELECT s.suburb,
         SUM(s.total_rent) AS rt,
         SUM(s.n_rented) AS rn,
         MAX(s.month) AS recent_month,
         COUNT(*) AS n_recent_m
  FROM suburb_rent s, maxym m
  WHERE EXTRACT(YEAR FROM s.month)*12 + EXTRACT(MONTH FROM s.month) >= m.mx - 5
  GROUP BY s.suburb
),
prev AS (
  SELECT s.suburb,
         SUM(s.total_rent) AS pt,
         SUM(s.n_rented) AS pn,
         COUNT(*) AS n_prev_m
  FROM suburb_rent s, maxym m
  WHERE EXTRACT(YEAR FROM s.month)*12 + EXTRACT(MONTH FROM s.month) >= m.mx - 17
    AND EXTRACT(YEAR FROM s.month)*12 + EXTRACT(MONTH FROM s.month) <= m.mx - 12
  GROUP BY s.suburb
)
SELECT r.suburb,
       r.recent_month,
       r.rn AS recent_bonds,
       r.rt/NULLIF(r.rn,0) AS recent_rent,
       p.pn AS prev_bonds,
       p.pt/NULLIF(p.pn,0) AS prev_rent,
       CASE WHEN p.pn IS NULL OR p.pn = 0 OR NULLIF(p.pt/NULLIF(p.pn,0),0) IS NULL THEN NULL
            ELSE (r.rt/NULLIF(r.rn,0) - p.pt/NULLIF(p.pn,0)) / (p.pt/NULLIF(p.pn,0)) * 100
       END AS growth_pct
FROM recent r
LEFT JOIN prev p ON r.suburb = p.suburb
ORDER BY growth_pct DESC
LIMIT 4000

You are a data-insight agent. You answer questions over whatever datasets the
marts schema exposes — do NOT assume a particular domain; discover what the data
is from the mart index and the knowledge base. Produce a clear, insightful
DATA-INSIGHT REPORT — not prose. You do the heavy lifting as CODE that calls
tested skills, not by stitching tools together.

Work in this order:
1. search_knowledge(query, why="..."): find the 1-2 relevant knowledge pages for this
   dataset/metric — the grain to pull, which columns mean what, join keys, and any
   gotchas. This is where dataset-specific rules live; always start here. You do
   NOT need knowledge for how to compute growth/yield or structure the report —
   that lives in the tested skills below; just call them.
2. describe_table('<schema.table>', why="..."): the prompt lists only table names + a
   one-line purpose, so read a table's exact columns here before you write SQL.
   You may need MORE THAN ONE table (e.g. a ratio across two marts) — pull each.
3. extract(sql, name, purpose, why="..."): pull ALL the data you need in ONE
   WIDE extract — SELECT month + the metric columns, filtered to the entity,
   PLUS the mart's explanatory attribute columns (e.g. a type or band) when
   they could explain the metric, AGGREGATED IN SQL to month x entity x
   attribute grain so it stays small. Later analysis passes slice this same
   frame — never extract again between report passes. KEEP EVERY MONTH (never
   add a `WHERE <count> >= N` filter). The result is loaded as a pandas
   DataFrame named `name` (default `df`); call extract again with a different
   `name` only when a SECOND TABLE is genuinely needed (e.g. a ratio across two
   marts), then join in SQL or in pandas. You get up to 8
   extracts. Use lookup_values first (FREE) to resolve a text value's exact
   spelling/casing. Do NOT spend an extract (or a turn) probing min/max month
   or row counts first — pull the series directly and read its span in pandas

4. run_analysis(code): write SHORT pandas that calls skills.* over the frame(s)
   and assigns the result to `result` (helpers: trend_series/growth_rate/
   latest_value as before, e.g. `s = skills.trend_series(df, month_col="month",

   The app STREAMS each page to the user the moment you finish it, so work in
   TWO SHORT PASSES over the frame(s) you already extracted (never re-extract):
   PASS 1 — the summary page (always FIRST, keep it FAST — no attribute
   slicing here): aggregate to headline level and assign

           summary="...",

       )
       Always include a latest_value + growth headline and the trend/comparison

   PASS 2 — the insights page (a SECOND run_analysis call, right after pass 1
   succeeds): slice the SAME frame by its attribute columns (e.g. a type or
   band; call driver_analysis when the question asks WHY or attributes exist)
   and assign
       result = skills.build_insights(insights=[
           skills.make_insight("...", "...", chart=skills.comparison_chart(...)),
       ])
       naming the strongest driver of the Page-1 numbers with a
       comparison_chart of its levels. It merges into the pass-1 report.
   You get up to 4 run_analysis attempts TOTAL across both passes; if
   a pass returns an error, fix the code and retry.
   NEVER do growth/yield/rolling maths yourself — call the skill. If NO skill fits,
   you MAY use pandas but you MUST call skills.skill_gap(need, why) naming what a
   future skill should do.
   Chart choice is also a skill choice: trend over time -> trend_chart; different
   scales on one axis -> dual_axis_chart; ranked comparisons -> comparison_chart;
   composition -> profile_chart; spread/outliers -> distribution_chart.
5. If the available marts genuinely cannot answer the question, call

6. Return a one-line confirmation string (the user sees the report, not this text).

DATA NOTE: month/date values arrive as plain STRINGS (e.g. "2026-05" or
"2026-05-01"), not datetimes. Use them directly in text — never apply a date
format spec (e.g. f"{m:%b %Y}" will fail); latest_value already returns a ready
"month" string for the basis.

RANKING ("top/best/fastest X"): an extract is capped at ~5000 rows,
so you usually CANNOT pull every month for every group (that truncates and
corrupts the series). Instead compute the ranking metric IN THE SQL extract — one
row per group — e.g. a CTE that computes each group's value in a recent window and

Available inside run_analysis (import-free; call as skills.<name>):

  gross_yield(rent_df, price_df, *, key_cols, weekly_rent_col, price_col)

  driver_analysis(df, *, dimensions, value_col, den_col=None, top=3)

         {"top_dimension", "overall", "ranked":[{dimension, score_pct, levels}]}.
         Use for "why/what drives X" and to power the Insights breakdown.
  # visualisation (consistent house style, validated)
  trend_chart(series_df, *, title=None) -> chart spec
  comparison_chart(df, *, category_col, value_col, title=None, series_col=None) -> chart spec
  dual_axis_chart(df, *, x_col, left_value_col, right_value_col, title=None,
                  left_title=None, right_title=None, x_type="temporal") -> chart spec
      -> bars + secondary-axis line for two metrics with different scales.
  distribution_chart(df, *, value_col, title=None, category_col=None) -> chart spec
      -> histogram for spread/outlier/distribution questions.
  profile_chart(df, *, category_col, segment_col, value_col, title=None, normalize=True)
      -> stacked composition bars (each entity's segment mix as % shares).
  # insight structure
  make_insight(heading, body, *, query_refs=None, chart=None) -> insight
  related_metrics([{label,value,basis}, ...]) -> related headline tiles
  data_table(df, *, columns, title=None, variant="plain", bar_key=None) -> table payload

         (ranked draws inline bars sized by bar_key) — for ranked lists / side-by-side
         comparisons that read better as rows than as a chart.
  build_report(*, summary, headlines=None, insights=None, profiles=None,
               main_chart=None, table=None) -> report
  build_insights(*, insights, profiles=None) -> pass-2 patch that merges insight

  # bootstrap: we start from ZERO skills — flag anything missing

Top 4 knowledge pages for 'property rent suburb growth':

### property-rent-overview  (domains/property-rent/overview.md) — full page inlined below (no need to read_knowledge)
# Property rent (dataset nsw_rent)

## Primary building block: `marts.property_rent`
One row per **postcode + property_type + bedroom_band + month** — there is
**no suburb column** (the rental-bond source has no locality). No precomputed growth.
- `postcode` (text), `property_type` (text: 'house'/'unit'), `bedroom_band` (text), `month` (date)
- `total_weekly_rent` (numeric) — sum of weekly_rent that month
- `n_rented` (int) — count of bonds that month
- `avg_weekly_rent` (numeric) — bucket-level average weekly rent
- `median_weekly_rent` (numeric) — bucket-level median weekly rent

Average rent = `total_weekly_rent / nullif(n_rented, 0)`.

## Resolving a suburb
Rent has no suburb, so a "rent in <suburb>" question must first map the suburb to
its postcode(s) via `staging.int_postcode_geo`
([[domains/property-sales/suburbs-and-postcodes]]), then query rent by postcode.

## Other tables
- `staging.property_rent` — record grain (~3M rows); only for record-level questions,
  always filtered by postcode/month.

## Reliability
Bond counts per postcode/month can be thin. **Do not filter thin months out** of a
trend with a `WHERE n_rented >= N` clause — keep every month and let the 6-month
rolling average absorb the noise (the `rolling_average` / `latest_value` skills
apply the 6-month window).

### suburbs-and-postcodes  (domains/property-sales/suburbs-and-postcodes.md) — full page inlined below (no need to read_knowledge)
# Suburbs and postcodes

- **Sales** carry a real `suburb` dimension (from the sale record). Filter by suburb
  for one locality. But postcode<->suburb is **not 1:1** — to get a postcode total,
  SUM `total_sale_value` / `n_sold` across that postcode's suburbs (additive);
  bucket medians are not additive.
- **Rent has NO suburb** (the source has no locality). For a rent-by-suburb
  question, resolve the suburb to its postcode(s) first via
  `staging.int_postcode_geo` (`WHERE suburb ILIKE '%name%'`), then query rent by
  postcode ([[domains/property-rent/overview]]).
- Join sales<->rent on **(postcode, property_type, month)**, never on suburb.

## Gotchas
- Suburb values are UPPERCASE in the marts ('HORNSBY', 'NORMANHURST'). Use the exact
  case or ILIKE — a mixed-case literal returns zero rows silently.
- A suburb may map to several postcodes and vice versa; decide whether the question
  is about the suburb (use the suburb dimension on sales) or the postcode (aggregate).

### property-sales-overview  (domains/property-sales/overview.md)
NSW property sales mart — table grain and the key columns to query.
> One row per **postcode + suburb + property_type + area_band + zoning + month**.
(read_knowledge('property-sales-overview') for the full page)

### one-pass-trend-analysis  (presentation/one-pass-trend-analysis.md)
Build a whole month-by-group trend answer in a single run_analysis pass.
> - rent: `total_weekly_rent / nullif(n_rented, 0)`

Table marts.property_rent — Aggregate mart for cleaned NSW rental bond lodgements. Physical table: marts.property_rent, matching raw.property_rent and staging.property_rent for easy lineage. One row per (postcode, property_type, bedroom_band, month). Rent source data has no suburb, so the honest aggregate grain is postcode-level. Holds cleaned attributes plus additive aggregate metrics so consumers can re-aggregate to higher levels and compute derived metrics such as rent growth or joined yield in SQL. No precomputed ALL rows or growth percentages. Belongs to the `nsw_rent` dataset (RLS-scoped). Verified by assert_property_rent_has_coverage and assert_property_rent_unique_postcode_type_bedroom_month.
Columns:
  postcode — Postcode. Join key to marts.property_sales with property_type and month when deriving yield.
  property_type — 'house' or 'unit'. No synthetic 'ALL' rows; re-aggregate across property_type when needed.
  bedroom_band — '0','1','2','3','4','5+', or 'unknown'. Part of the grain.
  month — Calendar month (first-of-month date) the bonds were lodged in.
  total_weekly_rent — Additive sum of weekly_rent (AUD) in the bucket. Use with n_rented for re-aggregated averages and growth.
  n_rented — Additive count of bonds in the bucket.
  avg_weekly_rent — Bucket-level average weekly rent. For re-aggregated means, recompute from sum(total_weekly_rent) / sum(n_rented).
  median_weekly_rent — Bucket-level median weekly rent. Useful for the current bucket, but not additive across buckets.
  min_weekly_rent — Minimum weekly rent in the bucket.
  max_weekly_rent — Maximum weekly rent in the bucket.

Table staging.int_postcode_geo — Postcode <-> suburb bridge: every (postcode, suburb) pair seen in the sale records, with a sale count. Does NOT collapse to one suburb per postcode — postcode <-> suburb is not 1:1, so every locality is present. Use it to resolve a suburb name to its postcode(s), especially for rent questions: marts.property_rent has no suburb (raw.property_rent has no locality), so "rent in <suburb>" means looking the suburb up here to get its postcode(s), then querying rent by postcode. Belongs to the `nsw_sales` dataset (RLS-scoped, since it's derived from sales).
Columns:
  postcode — Postcode.
  suburb — Suburb/locality sharing that postcode.
  n_sales — Number of sales carrying this postcode/suburb pairing (order by it desc for the dominant suburb).

# property-sales-overview
# Property sales (dataset nsw_sales)

## Primary building block: `marts.property_sales`
One row per **postcode + suburb + property_type + area_band + zoning + month**.
No precomputed growth.
- `postcode` (text) — join key to rent (with property_type, month)
- `suburb` (text) — real dimension; filter for one locality. Values are Title
  Case (e.g. 'Hornsby', 'Anabranch South') — resolve exact spellings with ONE
  lookup_values call (`pattern="A|B"` resolves several at once)
- `property_type` (text) — 'house' or 'unit'; no synthetic 'ALL' rows —
  [[domains/property-sales/property-types]]
- `area_band` (text) — cleaned lot-size band; part of the grain
- `zoning` (text) — planning zone or 'unknown'; part of the grain
- `month` (date) — first-of-month
- `total_sale_value` (numeric) — sum of sale_price that month
- `n_sold` (int) — count of sales that month
- `avg_sale_price` (numeric) — bucket-level average sale price
- `median_sale_price` (numeric) — bucket-level median sale price

Average price = `total_sale_value / nullif(n_sold, 0)` (composes across any window).
`total_sale_value` and `n_sold` are additive across postcode/suburb/property_type/
area/zoning buckets; bucket medians are NOT — do not sum medians.

## Other tables
- `staging.property_sales` — record grain, ~3M rows. Only for record-level questions
  (individual sales, addresses); always filter by postcode/month first.

## Reliability
Buckets are kept even when tiny. **Do not filter thin months out** of a trend or
series with a `WHERE n_sold >= N` clause — keep every month and let the 6-month
rolling average absorb the noise (the `rolling_average` / `latest_value` skills
apply the 6-month window). SELECT-only; RLS limits rows to the datasets the user
may access.

The question is "Which suburbs had the fastest rent growth last year?" I need to:

1. Map each suburb to its postcode(s) via `int_postcode_geo`
2. Aggregate rent by postcode across all property types / bedroom bands / months
3. Compute the suburb's rent growth as a postcode-aggregated rate

But a suburb can map to multiple postcodes and vice versa. To answer "suburbs with fastest rent growth", I should compute per-suburb rent growth. The cleanest approach: aggregate rent to suburb level.

Since a suburb may share a postcode with other suburbs, and postcodes may span multiple suburbs, I need a strategy. The knowledge notes: "postcode<->suburb is not 1:1". To compute per-suburb rent, I'll aggregate rent by postcode, then map each suburb to its postcode(s) and use the sum of rents across those postcodes for that suburb.

Actually, given suburban rents are best approximated at postcode grain, and a suburb could map to a set of postcodes, the suburb's rent = sum of rents across all its postcodes. This is the most sensible approach.

Let me get the data. I'll compute per-postcode monthly total rent (total_weekly_rent, n_rented summed across property_type and bedroom_band) from the rent mart, and pull the distinct postcodes per suburb from int_postcode_geo.

Approach for "last year" growth: Compare a recent window (latest 6 months) vs the same 6-month window roughly a year earlier. Since the rolling/growth skills apply in pandas, I'll extract monthly postcode-level rent series.

Let me structure the extract. I need per-suburb per-month rent. Let me join rent (postcode-level monthly aggregate) with the suburb->postcode bridge.

For ranking, rows cap ~5000. Number of suburbs could be large (NSW has many). But the bridge `int_postcode_geo` has every (postcode, suburb) pair. Let me check the size. Better approach per the RANKING guidance: compute the ranking metric IN SQL, one row per suburb.

Let me build a SQL extract that:
1. Aggregates rent mart to postcode x month: sum(total_weekly_rent), sum(n_rented)
2. Joins to int_postcode_geo to get suburb mapping
3. Aggregates to suburb x month (summing across postcodes)
4. Computes avg weekly rent per suburb-month = sum(total_weekly_rent)/sum(n_rented)
5. Computes rent in recent window vs year earlier, and growth pct

But "last year" - I need to determine what window. Let me use the growth_rate approach on the monthly series rather than hardcoding windows in SQL. Actually, given the ranking needs to be done in SQL (row cap), I should compute growth in SQL.

However, I don't know the date span yet. Let me think about a robust SQL: compute for each suburb, recent average monthly rent (over the latest 6 months available) vs the average over the same 6-month period one year prior (or the earliest 6 months if not enough data). 

Actually a cleaner approach that works regardless of exact span: For each suburb, compute a "current" 6-month average rent (latest available 6 months) and a "year-ago" 6-month average. Since I need comparable periods, let me use the max month to anchor.

Let me instead do a two-level approach:
- Extract 1: suburb x month weekly-rent series (agg from rent mart joined to bridge). This gives the full monthly series per suburb.

But the row cap issue: too many suburbs. Let me limit to suburbs with meaningful data. The ranking-guidance says compute in SQL with one row per group.

Let me write a single SQL extract computing per-suburb growth. I'll first check the max month in rent data to anchor the windows. Actually I should avoid probing first. Let me just extract the suburb x month series but cap to a reasonable set — but that truncates.

```sql
WITH rent_by_postcode AS (
  SELECT postcode,
         month,
         SUM(total_weekly_rent) AS total_rent,
         SUM(n_rented) AS n_rented
  FROM marts.property_rent
  GROUP BY postcode, month
),
suburb_rent AS (
  SELECT g.suburb,
         r.month,
         SUM(r.total_rent) AS total_rent,
         SUM(r.n_rented) AS n_rented
  FROM rent_by_postcode r
  JOIN staging.int_postcode_geo g ON r.postcode = g.postcode
  GROUP BY g.suburb, r.month
),
recent AS (
  SELECT suburb,
         SUM(total_rent)/NULLIF(SUM(n_rented),0) AS recent_rent,
         COUNT(*) AS n_months_recent
  FROM suburb_rent
  WHERE month >= DATEADD(month, -6+1, (SELECT MAX(month) FROM suburb_rent))
  -- anchor to max month
  GROUP BY suburb
),
...
```

Hmm, this is getting complex. Let me use a slightly simpler, robust approach for the SQL ranking. 

Actually, let me reconsider. There are two "last year" interpretations. Rent growth over the past 12 months (year-over-year). The `growth_rate` skill computes % growth over `years` on the 6-month rolling base. 

Given the RANKING guidance, I should compute growth in SQL as one row per suburb (capped fine). Let me write a CTE-based extract that computes for each suburb the 6-month average rent ending at the max month and the 6-month average ending 12 months prior, then growth pct.

Let me write the SQL carefully. I'll use the max month from the data as anchor. To identify "last year", I compare the most recent 6-month window to the 6-month window ending ~12 months earlier.

Let me define: 
- `max_month` = MAX(month) over all
- recent window: months from (max_month - 5 months) to max_month (latest 6 full months)
- year-ago window: months from (max_month - 17 months) to (max_month - 12 months)

This ensures exactly 12 months apart.

```sql

  SELECT postcode, month,
         SUM(total_weekly_rent) AS total_rent,
         SUM(n_rented) AS n_rented
  FROM marts.property_rent
  GROUP BY postcode, month
),
suburb_rent AS (
  SELECT g.suburb, r.month,
         SUM(r.total_rent) AS total_rent,
         SUM(r.n_rented) AS n_rented
  FROM rent_by_postcode r
  JOIN staging.int_postcode_geo g ON r.postcode = g.postcode
  GROUP BY g.suburb, r.month
),
recent AS (
  SELECT suburb,
         SUM(total_rent) AS rt, SUM(n_rented) AS rn,
```
